evidence_basis: PREPRINT, NOT PEER REVIEWED. Nothing here may raise the status of any claim.

THE ONLY SOURCE IN THIS GROUP THAT MOVES WWOX IN BOTH DIRECTIONS IN ONE MODEL. Down: two independent UAS-RNAi constructs under pan-neuronal, pan-glial and clock drivers. Up: CRISPR activation at the Wwox transcription start site giving about a two-fold mRNA increase measured by qPCR, and separately a UAS-cDNA of fly or human WWOX.
THE UP-ARM IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART AND ITS DOSE IS MEASURED ONLY AS TRANSCRIPT. No WWOX protein level is reported anywhere in the preprint.

KNOCKDOWN WITHOUT AMYLOID shortens median lifespan (neuronal 57 to 42 and 40 days, pan-glial 74 to 70) and increases sleep without disturbing circadian rhythmicity; startle-induced climbing is unaffected, which is an internal negative the authors state.

KNOCKDOWN WITH AMYLOID is synergistic rather than additive by Cox proportional-hazards modelling (interaction p below 0.0001), median lifespan 41 to 26 and 24 days, and raises total amyloid-beta-42 (p = 0.033) led by the SOLUBLE fraction (p = 0.0024) with the insoluble fraction only trending (p = 0.0602) and no change in aggregate number or size. Glial knockdown with neuronal amyloid barely moves lifespan and does not move locomotion, so the relevant pool is neuronal.

MECHANISM, AND A NEGATIVE THAT BEARS DIRECTLY ON THE WWOX-HIF1A LITERATURE: lactate dehydrogenase transcript and L-lactate rise as the single interaction metabolite, lactate dehydrogenase knockdown RESCUES the climbing deficit, Atf4 protein rises (p = 0.0022), and the HIF1-alpha homologue reporter sima:GFP does NOT change (p = 0.5185), nor does Xbp1 splicing. The route named is PERK-Atf4, not HIF1-alpha. Brain ATP is unchanged.

UPREGULATION RESCUES AND DOES NOT SIMPLY RUN THE MECHANISM BACKWARDS. With amyloid, CRISPR activation moves median lifespan from 29 to 47.5 days (p below 0.0001), rescues climbing, and lowers plaque size (p = 0.0003) and number (p = 0.0071) and both amyloid fractions; human WWOX cDNA reproduces the lifespan rescue. But the rescue does not restore lactate: its only interaction metabolite is L-methionine, down, with seven cysteine and methionine metabolism transcripts down. In a control background the same upregulation changes nothing.

TRANSFER LIMITS: Drosophila, with no CNS myelin and no myelin endpoint of any kind; RNA interference is not one null allele and no heterozygous fly is studied; the AD attribution is a GWAS and eQTL statement about an intergenic variant between WWOX and MAF, not a statement about WWOX-DEE; and every rescue arm is concurrent rather than applied after pathology is established.

Lactate dehydrogenase is bidirectionally constrained in this literature by the preprint's own account, since its knockdown is also reported detrimental in fly amyloid models, so lowering lactate is not a safe target derived from this work.
Deposition is a strength worth recording against other preprints: ArrayExpress E-MTAB-14948 and E-MTAB-14949 and MetaboLights MTBLS12344 are named, with analysis code on a public repository.
Supplemental Tables S1 to S7 were persisted but not opened row by row, and supplementary figure panels were read from their legends rather than as images, so the reading is partial.

evidence_basis: PREPRINT, NOT PEER REVIEWED. Nothing in this reading may raise the status of any claim, and the label travels with every statement drawn from it.

THE ALLELE AND ITS LIMIT. In vivo the conditional is Olig2-Cre crossed to a Wwox flox/flox allele with loxP sites adjoining exon 1; that is an oligodendroglial-LINEAGE deletion from development, not an inducible or OPC-timed one. The in vitro arm that carries the phrase cell-autonomous uses primary OPC cultures from CONSTITUTIVE Wwox-null pups, not from the conditional. Cell autonomy is therefore established for the lineage and by culture isolation, not for an adult OPC that lost WWOX as an adult.

THE BASELINE PHENOTYPE IS NEARLY ABSENT, WHICH IS THE RESULT THAT MATTERS FOR A DOSE MODEL. In O-KO mice at baseline the proportions of PDGFR-alpha-positive OPCs and CC1-positive oligodendrocytes are unchanged, cortical and callosal MBP immunofluorescence is comparable, and myelinated-axon counts per field of view do not differ (117.6 plus-minus 12.5 versus 125.1 plus-minus 9, P = 0.22). Only myelin thickness is subtly reduced. The oligodendroglial requirement is unmasked by challenge, not by development.

AGEING AND CUPRIZONE UNMASK IT. At 18 months myelinated axons fall (130.1 plus-minus 28.6 versus 102.3 plus-minus 31.8, P = 0.0044). After five weeks of 0.2 percent cuprizone and two weeks of recovery, demyelination itself is comparable between genotypes while remyelination is not: MBP intensity 60 versus 40, myelinated axons per field 59.1 versus 36.1, CC1-positive cells 220 versus 140, OPCs 78.25 versus 111.

MECHANISM AS STATED: SOX10 carries a PPxY motif; endogenous WWOX-SOX10 co-immunoprecipitation from HA-tagged knock-in cortex; GST pull-down shows dose-dependent SOX10 increase with WWOX that a WW1-domain mutant (WFPA) abolishes; cycloheximide chase shows faster SOX10 decay in a CRISPR Wwox-KO Oli-neu line, with MG132 rescuing in both genotypes; ubiquitinated SOX10 is described by the authors themselves as a modest increase.

THE PREPRINT DOES NOT CLAIM TO CONTRADICT THE NEURONAL-DELETION PAPER AND SAYS SO: 'While previous studies suggest that neuronal deletion of WWOX leads to hypomyelination via a non-cell autonomous mechanism, our data demonstrate that oligodendroglia-specific deletion results in a distinct phenotype.' It also keeps a non-cell-autonomous contribution open for mature oligodendrocytes and for axonal cues.
EARNED NULL ON THE CARRIER QUESTION: Wwox heterozygous mice are named in the Methods as existing in the colony and are used in no experiment here.

STATISTICAL LIMITS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: snRNA-seq uses two, two and three pooled samples per genotype-condition and tests differential abundance against SIMULATED replicates obtained by sampling 33 percent of nuclei without replacement, which resamples the same animals rather than replicating them; the baseline MBP comparison rests on two mice per genotype; and the Methods set significance at p below 0.005 while the figure stars are defined at 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001.

The corresponding author declares consultancy for a therapeutics company. Data availability is 'upon publication' with no accession.

evidence_basis: Forty female cynomolgus macaques aggregated from two toxicology studies, 12-50 months at dosing, pre-selected for the LOWEST anti-capsid titres - the exact complement of the seropositive-stratified study read beside it, so the two must not be pooled. Zero occurrences of WWOX.

The design carries the arms the rest of the wave lacks: empty capsid, promoterless vector and full vector at a comparable capsid dose, plus a low/high dose pair. Liver and DRG toxicity occurred ONLY with the full expressing vector. This is the cleanest separation of capsid exposure from expression-driven injury in the wave.

Counterweight recorded from the same paper: vector genome load was highest in the injured tissues while transgene transcript was highest in uninjured heart and skeletal muscle, so expression MAGNITUDE does not predict which tissue is injured. This is in tension with the review in this same group attributing DRG toxicity to supraphysiological expression level; the tension is recorded, not harmonised.

NfL rising with DRG single-cell necrosis, peaking day 28, is the wave's candidate blood-measurable correlate of a necropsy-only lesion - but it is CITED to the authors' own prior report and is not measured in this paper. Logged as an open reading debt.

The animals received no immunosuppression; the authors note the identified interferon axis signals through JAK/STAT rather than NF-kappa-B and offer this as a reason glucocorticoids may be insufficient prophylaxis. Recorded as the authors' hypothesis, since no immunosuppressed arm was run.
Figures 1-8 read as captions only; supplementary Figures S1-S6 and Tables S1-S12 NOT fetched, including Figure S1 which carries the biodistribution and expression data behind the dissociation above.

evidence_basis: Twenty cynomolgus macaques, 10 male and 10 female - the only sex-balanced study in the group - lumbar intrathecal over approximately 6 hours via implanted catheter, necropsy at 6 and 12 weeks. Cargo is a U6-driven knockdown microRNA, the opposite direction from a restoration programme. Zero occurrences of WWOX.

FIGURE 5 WAS RENDERED AND READ AT PANEL LEVEL and is declared as an artefact. The Figure 5A caption states treated DRG show no significant histological abnormality; the BODY reports lesions in 40 per cent of animals. The panel supports the body. The caption's qualifier 'representative' carries the whole discrepancy, and the manifest records the contradiction as a pointed locator pair.

The load-bearing number is in the control arm: two of four saline animals also had minimal-to-mild DRG lesions. Together with the vehicle-group finding in the companion primate study, two independent NHP studies in this group show the lesions attributed to intrathecal AAV9 also occur in vehicle-dosed macaques.

Three internal quantity contradictions found: the low NHP dose is printed as 6E13 in both Results and Methods but as 5E13 in the Figure 5A row labels (verified at 800 per cent magnification); the infusion volume is 4 mL in Results and 3 mL in Methods; the Figure 5A scale bars are given in millimetres in the caption where the panel prints micrometres.

Transferable monitoring design: serial nerve conduction velocity and compound muscle action potential at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks, plus troponin I, ECG and ophthalmic examination - functional, non-terminal and performable in a patient.

NfL is used here as a marker of therapeutic BENEFIT (decreasing), where the companion study uses it as a marker of vector TOXICITY (increasing). Recorded as a limit on NfL's specificity in any disease that itself causes axonal loss.

evidence_basis: Narrative review with no primary measurement of its own. Zero occurrences of WWOX. The Orchestrator called it the weakest member of the group and said to drop it first; it is in fact the only source in the group that carries the HUMAN evidence base, which is what the group's question asks for.
TABLE 1 read in full and CELL-WISE from the XML table structure; the clinical-application sections were read in full; the preclinical rodent and large-animal sections were read by title only.

The regulatory fact that governs the whole group: primate DRG histopathology prompted a regulatory hold on enrolment in a human paediatric intrathecal programme using this capsid and route, and that study was stopped before its high-dose cohort filled.

Human DRG outcome, from the same source: where a signal appeared it was sensory, mild and improved with symptomatic treatment; at the HIGHEST human intrathecal doses reported, two separate programmes assessed DRG by MRI and nerve conduction studies and found nothing. The human record therefore does not scale monotonically with dose.

The transferable pattern: four independent programmes adopt triple immunosuppression where the recipient is predicted null for the transgene product, versus a steroid alone where endogenous protein is present. A biallelic loss-of-function recipient falls in the predicted-null class by construction.

A paragraph reporting hepatotoxicity percentages is internally incoherent as printed - it compares one route to itself, gives a sham-control rate exceeding the treated rate, and contains a typographical error - so none of its four percentages may be carried. The same paragraph calls a study single-arm while listing its sham groups.

Self-correction recorded: an inference I formed from the prose - that intrathecal dosing is not used below age two - is contradicted by Table 1, which lists trials enrolling from the first months of life. The approved indication begins at two years; trials do not.

Every datum in this source is secondary and none of the cited primaries was read; the references behind the named programmes and behind the primate study that triggered the hold are open reading debts.

evidence_basis: WHY THIS IS partial_fulltext_read AND NOT complete, stated first so it is not over-read: every section of the article, every figure panel, the whole 21-page supplementary PDF with its nine figures, and all three supplementary spreadsheets row by row were read, and the 64 references were enumerated and resolved. What was NOT done is the two supplementary videos: eight frames were sampled from each with a bundled ffmpeg and no genotype is identifiable on any frame, so their content is owed. The references were screened and resolved, not read as sources.

ARTEFACT: the operator-supplied typeset PDF (17 pages, sha256 113522bb09b42a2dc0252bc1d7b112b66e3a68323ab1348c042f0ac8c8e8fa4c) and the complete supplementary archive (sha256 cfb264e45a6d6e2d7082853de293431594c8235cf087fbecbd0b3fcf1956c276) are the article's own pages and its full supplement, which the laboratory had never held. The derived text layer declared as source_locator is REFUSED as a quote surface: the validator's screen returns SUSPECT with 24 C0 controls, first U+0018 at offset 6970, and the journal's familiar printable damage is all present (P 5 0.05 for P < 0.05, fold change 41.5 for > 1.5, delta (55 Hz) for (<5 Hz), P 4 0.01 for P <= 0.01, Greek letters dropped). Every article locator is therefore rendered_text or figure on a page rendered from the declared PDF digest. The supplement's derived text screens CLEAN and its locators are matched against it exactly.

WITHDRAWAL OF A PRIOR FINDING, ON THE SAME BYTES. FTR-20260923-33914858-01 recorded that the legend of Supplementary Fig. 3 was MISSING from File009 and that the paper's neocortical-origin claim therefore had no n, ages or depths on any held surface. File009 here carries the SAME sha256 as the file that receipt names and DOES contain that legend: 1125 bursts across all layers, 149 / 834 / 142 in three S-KO examples, over 100-200 s of recording. The earlier absence was a property of that reading's extraction, not of the document. The finding is retired rather than carried.

DIGEST DISCREPANCY RECORDED, NOT RESOLVED: FTR-20260923-33914858-01 names File010.mp4 as sha256 2ef48d089be350fb3bef68799c443305b9ca9124ea318066f6a2fad8607ecb3c; this archive's member is 87ec870a96251af9ee3211d4b7b0599360d1a035c2e1cbd41ca46ced6adf52bd. Two byte-level instances of that member exist. File011 and the three spreadsheets and File009 match the earlier receipt exactly. The earlier artefact is absent from the checkout, so the two cannot be compared.

THE MYELIN QUANTITIES, WITH THE UNIT OF THE TEST, WHICH IS THE PART USUALLY DROPPED. Corpus callosum at P17, myelinated axons per field: S-KO 55 plus-minus 35 against S-Control 180 plus-minus 40. Optic nerve, unmyelinated axons per field: 270 plus-minus 60 against 55 plus-minus 20. g-ratio significantly higher in both tracts. CC1-positive mature oligodendrocytes reduced about two-fold with significantly more PDGFR-alpha-positive OPCs, counted in 0.5 mm2 over three sections. Every one of these comes from n = 3 animals per genotype, yet each panel plots 13 to 15 points and the asterisks are computed over FIELDS OF VIEW, not animals. The Figure 5B legend's axon totals do not reconcile with its own points either: thirteen S-KO fields averaging about 55 axons is roughly 700, not the 1200 the legend states.

THE RUNNING TEXT INFLATES ITS OWN FOLD CHANGES, CONSISTENTLY AND IN ONE DIRECTION. It prints about 3.5 to 4-fold fewer myelinated axons and about 6-fold more unmyelinated optic-nerve axons. The authors' own averages give 3.3-fold and 4.9-fold; the panel means read at 600 dpi give about 3.3-fold and about 4.2-fold. Both roundings enlarge the effect and neither is within rounding distance of the printed claim.

THE OLIGODENDROCYTE-DEATH NEGATIVE IS AN IMAGE, NOT A MEASUREMENT: CC1 with cleaved caspase-3 at P18, with no count, no n and no test anywhere in the paper or the supplement. The maturation-block reading leans on it.

THE HETEROZYGOTE ARM, EXHAUSTIVELY. The Synapsin-Cre heterozygote appears in four places and nowhere else: slice bursting (0 of 11 control slices from seven animals; 4 of 23 S-HT slices from fourteen animals; 36 of 42 S-KO slices from twenty-four animals, with the Figure 2B legend restating the same experiment per ANIMAL as about 20 and 84 percent, which resolves the discrepancy wave 4 flagged); spectral power, where S-HT is present only as the comparator of the homozygote; the evoked response in Figure 2F, where the first peak carries only an S-Control-versus-S-KO bracket; and Supplementary Fig. 3B, a single-animal depth series with no quantification. NO statistical comparison of either heterozygote against its control is reported on any measure, and no myelin, imaging, electron-microscopy or quantified behavioural endpoint exists for a heterozygote.

A WAVE-4 SENTENCE IS TOO STRONG AND IS REPAIRED BY THE SOURCE. The wave-4 reading recorded that no behavioural endpoint is reported for the heterozygote AT ALL. The paper does assert one - the heterozygote carrying one intact allele did not show any abnormal phenotypes and was behaviourally indistinguishable from control mice - with no data, no n and no test. ASSERTED BUT NOT MEASURED is a different and weaker object than ABSENT. The Nestin heterozygote gets the same treatment and the authors then read it across to human carriers, aligning an unmeasured mouse null with an unmeasured human null.

PANEL 2D CARRIES A BOUND NO SENTENCE IN THE PAPER STATES: in vivo the heterozygote spectrum runs at or above the homozygote's below about 5 Hz, while in vitro it runs BELOW the control. The heterozygote is not a clean intermediate on this measure and the direction of its departure differs between preparations.

CELL AUTONOMY: WHAT EACH CONDITIONAL ACTUALLY SHOWS. Nestin-Cre deletes in neural stem and progenitor cells and reproduces the null phenotype with its own electron-microscopy counts (myelinated axons per field 45 plus-minus 26 against 148 plus-minus 45; unmyelinated optic-nerve axons 440 plus-minus 210 against 195 plus-minus 35, n = 3, P18, and the knockout spread is half its own mean). Synapsin-Cre deletes in differentiated neurons and carries the whole phenotype. Olig2-Cre and GFAP-Cre are reported as flat negatives, and the Olig2 arm - the one that licenses the word non-cell-autonomous - consists of survival and weight to about 120 days (O-Control n = 11, O-KO n = 10, log-rank P exactly 1.0), a hind-limb clasping image, and ONE UNQUANTIFIED MBP COMPARISON AT P17. No electron microscopy, no g-ratio, no axon count, no CC1 or OPC count, no electrophysiology and no later age exists for the O-KO. A subtle, challenge-dependent or late myelin phenotype could not have been seen by anything that was done, and the authors themselves write that they cannot exclude a cell-autonomous oligodendrocyte function.

TWO FURTHER LIMITS ON THE CELL-AUTONOMY ARGUMENT, FROM THE PAPER'S OWN PAGES. The in-vitro arm uses EMBRYONIC DORSAL ROOT GANGLION neurons from the CONSTITUTIVE NULL, not Synapsin-Cre cortical neurons - a different genotype and a different neuron class from the in-vivo phenotype it explains, with n = 4 per condition from two experiments. And the deletion is incomplete in cortex at transcript level: Supplementary Table 1's per-sample columns give residual Wwox normalised counts of 172.7, 187.0 and 331.4 in S-KO cortex against 18.8, 18.8 and 28.0 in S-KO hippocampus, which is expected from non-neuronal cells in a cortical sample and is never stated, while cortex is where the myelin-intensity quantification is done.

THE HUMAN ORGANOID RESULT, WITH ITS n. CRISPR knockout of WWOX in a human embryonic stem cell line differentiated to oligocortical spheroids: resting membrane potential minus 52.1 plus-minus 0.90 mV in wild type (n = 3 organoids) against minus 21.28 plus-minus 6.91 mV in the knockout (n = 4); low-frequency power area under the curve 0.0285 against 0.0541; CC1 and CNP positive cells reduced at weeks 14, 20 and 30 with OPC markers unchanged or slightly up; and a week-37 electron-microscopy percentage bar built from n = 2 wild-type and n = 3 knockout organoids with no error bar and no test. Bounds that belong to the datum: the pair is a knockout and its parental line, not an isogenic patient allele; both genotypes are explicitly immature at week 15 and the authors read the potential difference as developmental delay; the knockout's dispersion is 7.7 times the wild type's; and it is the same laboratory, so it is convergence, not independent replication.

FIVE TEXT-VERSUS-PANEL DISCREPANCIES, THE FIRST OF WHICH REVERSES A PRINTED PAIR OF NUMBERS. (1) The Supplementary Fig. 6B legend says cells are significantly reduced in S-KO (12 plus-minus 4) compared to the S-Control (7 plus-minus 3), while the bar chart above it plots the control at about 13 and the S-KO at about 6.8: the direction is right and the two values are transposed. (2) and (3) are the two inflated fold changes. (4) The myelination gene-ontology term the text calls a significant downregulation sits on a negative-regulation false-discovery-rate scale of 0.09 to 0.11, which passes a conventional 0.25 and fails 0.05, and the paper states no threshold; the same panel's twelve up-regulated terms are all spliceosome, RNA-splicing, centromere and proteasome terms the text never mentions. (5) The evoked-response sentence claims the homozygote exceeds both control and heterozygote while panel 2F marks the first peak only against the control.

SPREADSHEET RECOUNT, AND THE HEADLINE DIFFERENTIAL-EXPRESSION COUNT IS AN UNADJUSTED ONE. The paper's 730 upregulated and 579 downregulated genes reproduce EXACTLY from Supplementary Table 1 on the raw p-value below 0.01 with fold change above 1.5; the same filter on the authors' own shrunken estimate gives 488 and 388, and on the ADJUSTED p-value it gives 281 and 280. The paper states no multiple-comparison correction anywhere and tests everything with a two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test. Of the 23 genes the running text lists as significantly downregulated, two fail an adjusted threshold of 0.01 in the authors' own table: Enpp2 at 0.281 and Myrf at 0.134 - and Myrf is the myelin regulatory factor the maturation-block reading leans on.

THE POOLED HIPPOCAMPAL TABLE UN-POOLS, AND THE THREE GENOTYPES ARE SATURATED RATHER THAN GRADED: residual Wwox normalised counts are 28.3 and 32.5 in the constitutive null, 5.1 and 25.5 in the Nestin conditional and 32.5, 33.0 and 49.0 in the Synapsin conditional, against 294 to 307 in wild type. The single pooled log2 fold change of minus 3.14 describes none of the three alleles, and the per-genotype comparison the authors could have made is available in their own deposit and is not made.

REAGENTS, READ ROW BY ROW: nineteen primer pairs, all oligodendrocyte and myelin genes, with NO Wwox pair and no housekeeping pair although the supplementary methods name HPRT or UBC; ten primaries, of which the anti-WWOX row carries catalogue N.A and an EMPTY source cell in a table whose nine other rows are populated; and only three secondaries, with NO anti-rabbit secondary at all although four primaries are rabbit and all four are imaged in published panels, and no DAPI or Hoechst although Hoechst is labelled in two figures.

WHAT THE PAPER DOES NOT SAY, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: no heterozygote-versus-control test on any measure; no multiple-comparison correction; no sex-split analysis (sex appears once, as either male or female in the electrophysiology methods); NO WWOX IMMUNOBLOT ANYWHERE - every WWOX measurement in the paper is immunofluorescence or transcript; no seizure frequency and no unanaesthetised electroencephalography, the in-vivo recordings being under ketamine-xylazine and the only unanaesthetised seizure data six videotaped animals with a duration; no deposited sequencing data; nothing about remyelination, repair or any age beyond about four weeks; and no test, in any model, of whether rescuing myelin rescues seizures or the reverse - the authors write that why hypomyelination should cause local hyperexcitability remains unclear.

A SECOND PRIOR FINDING CORRECTED: FTR-20260923-33914858-01 recorded an earned zero for a data-availability statement. Figure 4, the paper's only immunoblot image, carries four lane pairs (HET-1A, SCC-15, Tumor Tissue, Normal Tissue) and no siRNA lane at all; beta-actin is the only loading control for both fractions and no nuclear marker is blotted. The Table 4 ratios that carry the paper's title come from a blot the reader never sees, with no replicate count, no dispersion and no p value.

THE SILENCING WAS DONE IN A NON-CANCER OESOPHAGEAL LINE. WWOX siRNA was transfected into HET-1A, which the paper's own table captions call a human oesophageal squamous epithelial line; the head-and-neck cancer line SCC-15 was never silenced. The title's disease context is not the system the experiment was run in.

NO WNT OUTPUT IS MEASURED ANYWHERE. Beta-catenin, TCF/LEF reporter activity and every Wnt target gene are absent from the paper, so the step from nuclear Dvl to canonical Wnt activation is cited, never measured here.

ARITHMETIC. The reported '10%, 90% and 10%' increases reconcile with Table 4 for Dvl-2 (+96% on the nucleus/cytoplasm ratio) and Dvl-3 (+13.5%) but not for Dvl-1, which is +22.8% on that ratio, +15.4% on the nuclear fraction and -18.6% on the published C/N ratio: no formula yields 10%.

evidence_basis: Body, Tables 1-3 and all six figure legends read from the persisted JATS XML. Figure panels 1a and 1b (transcript axes) and 6a-6b (immunohistochemistry score distributions) inspected as pixels from the fingerprinted publisher rasters. Figure 5 was persisted and fingerprinted but its panels were not adjudicated, and the panels of Figures 2-4 were taken through their captions only; coverage.figures is therefore captions_only and the depth is partial, not complete.

The single supplementary file (uncropped Western blots) was retrieved from the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles archive, its served MD5 matched the MD5 the article's own JATS declares for that file, and its one page was rendered at 300 dpi and read panel by panel.

WWOX content: 257 occurrences in the body; the paper's entire method is the measurement of WWOX, in canine cutaneous mast cell tumour tissue and canine/murine mast cell lines. Four read-outs: comparative-Ct transcript normalised to 18S; immunoblot densitometry of a ~47 kDa band normalised to beta-actin at 43 kDa on a stripped-and-reprobed membrane; tissue immunohistochemistry scored on two ordinal scales by two blinded pathologists with measured weighted kappa 0.264 (intensity) and 0.273 (percent positivity); and a gain/loss-of-function arm that is an earned negative for proliferation and viability, with one significant clonogenic-survival point after knockdown at 6 Gy (p = 0.0416) and no significance at 4 Gy (p = 0.1200).

No analytical or clinical performance figure is stated anywhere: no limit of detection, no linear range, no calibrator, no sensitivity, no specificity, no cut-off. The sensitivity 78-94 percent and specificity 88-93 percent quoted in the Results belong to a cited copy-number study by other authors, not to any WWOX measurement made here. Neither antibody is validated against a genetic negative; the immunohistochemistry negative control is an isotype-matched irrelevant antibody.

Panel readings that bound the authors' text: Figure 1a shows group-level separation with individual-level overlap, three tumour samples equalling or exceeding the higher of the two normal mast-cell preparations; Figure 1b is drawn on a broken axis; Figure 6b separates the two tumour grades completely while Figure 6a overlaps, so the metric that separates is the one with the weaker inter-rater agreement; and the uncropped Figure 2A membrane shows the empty-vector and WWOX-overexpressing lanes at comparable intensity, with two further unlabelled lanes comparable to both.

Earned null for the disease question: the paper says nothing about brain, neurons, glia, epilepsy, neurodevelopment, any WWOX variant or allele, any zygosity, any body fluid, or WWOX enzymatic activity. Every matrix is tumour tissue or cultured cells.

Design: ten single-stranded AAV9-EGFP vectors differing only in promoter, each given as one 5 microlitre intracerebroventricular injection to C57Bl/6 neonates at postnatal day 0 to 1, necropsy at four weeks and two promoters also at eight weeks; ten animals per construct for assays plus three for whole-organ imaging, with four groups smaller. Read-outs: EGFP mRNA by RT-qPCR against Actin, whole-organ fluorescence declared qualitative only by the authors, quantitative western blot, and immunofluorescence colocalisation with NeuN, GFAP, S100B and Olig2.

Measured ranking by brain-area coverage: CAG 42 percent, p546 41 percent, CNP 37 percent, gfa1405 35 percent, GFAP about 24 percent, gfaABC(1)D 9 percent, EFS 5 to 9 percent, tCAG 5.8 percent, MAG 5.5 percent, rMBP 2 to 4 percent. Mean EGFP intensity in relative fluorescence units: CAG 474.8, gfa1405 412.1, GFAP 387.7, p546 154.0, gfaABC(1)D 91.54, CNP 45.51, MAG 9.548, tCAG 8.443, rMBP 3.258, EFS 2.678.

Measured cell-type colocalisation as a percentage of EGFP-positive cells: astrocyte marker S100B gave CAG 36, p546 1.9, GFAP 44, gfaABC(1)D 58 and gfa1405 37.7 percent; neuronal marker NeuN gave CAG 27, p546 72, GFAP 13, gfaABC(1)D 19 and gfa1405 11.9 percent. The oligodendrocyte promoter CNP reached up to 16 percent Olig2 and 21 to 29 percent NeuN, leaving about half of transduced cells unidentified; MAG reached up to 65 percent Olig2 and 13.5 percent NeuN.

The finding that bounds the cell-specific-promoter argument: the astrocyte-restricted gfa1405 produced robust hepatic EGFP transcript and, by quantitative western blot, the most hepatic EGFP protein of any promoter tested, while whole-organ fluorescence in liver showed minimal signal. The Discussion's liver reassurance addresses CAG, whose hepatic protein was minimal, and does not return to gfa1405.

Headroom: the new 1405 base-pair astrocyte promoter saves 803 base pairs against full-length GFAP and the authors state it maximises the accommodating transgene length to 2.3 kilobases inside a declared 4.8 kilobase single-stranded AAV packaging capacity.

Methodological caution recorded: the doses are not matched across arms of this head-to-head comparison, spanning 7.0 to 8.5 times ten to the tenth vector genomes per animal, about a 21 percent spread, with no adjustment. There is no dose-response, no adult animal, no large animal, no therapeutic transgene, no immunology, no toxicity and no functional outcome.

Supplementary Document S1, which carries the western-blot quantification behind the hepatic-protein finding and the full pairwise promoter comparison table, was not retrieved; coverage.supplementary is not_read and the depth is partial, not complete. Figure panels were not adjudicated and all six legends were read, so coverage.figures is captions_only.

Design: five capsid point mutations from two previously published liver-de-targeted AAV9 variants were combined into one capsid. Single-stranded genomes encoding firefly luciferase under a ubiquitous chicken beta-actin promoter were packaged into the parent capsid and three variants and given at 1 times ten to the eleventh vector genomes per animal by tail vein to C57BL/6 mice, with whole-animal bioluminescence at 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 weeks and necropsy at 9 weeks for vector genome quantitative PCR and transgene reverse-transcription quantitative PCR in liver, heart, gastrocnemius, brain and spinal cord.

The manufacturability cost the title does not carry: from the same producer-cell input the parent capsid yielded 3.58 times ten to the thirteenth vector genomes, the two single-parent variants about 2.0 times ten to the thirteenth, and the combined capsid 4.5 times ten to the twelfth, an eight-fold drop in packaging yield against the parent.

The liver result, which is the paper's strongest: the combined capsid gave about a 127-fold reduction in hepatic vector genome copies against the parent, the largest of any variant tested, together with the lowest hepatic transcript ratio.

The central text-versus-data tension: the summary states the capsid has reduced liver and heart tropism while minimally affecting CNS tropism, but the Discussion states the measurement plainly as all mutated capsids resulting in significantly lower vector genome copies in brain than the parent, with relative expression levels consistent among capsids. In spinal cord vector genomes were equivalent to the parent. Whole-animal peak average radiance fell from 7.3 times ten to the seventh for the parent to 5.8 times ten to the fifth for the combined capsid, about two orders of magnitude less total transgene signal at the same dose.

Vector genome copies and transgene expression disagreed in three of five tissues, and the authors propose the capsid itself may modulate transgene transcription, citing recent work on AAV9 capsid-promoter interaction, and call the mechanism undetermined. Expression from the combined capsid also declined significantly at weeks 6 and 9 against its own week-3 value.

Absences that bound the safety argument: no toxicity, histopathology, liver-enzyme, complement, cytokine or immunology measurement of any kind, no pre-existing-immunity or neutralising-antibody data for the new capsid surface, no dose-response, no large animal or primate, no cerebrospinal-fluid route, no therapeutic transgene and no cell-type resolution in brain. The dose-ceiling claim is therefore entirely inferential: nothing in the paper measures a toxicity threshold before or after the modification.

Figure panels were not adjudicated and all five captions were read, so coverage.figures is captions_only and the depth is partial, not complete. The article declares no separate supplementary file, so coverage.supplementary is not_present.

Design: a retrospective pooling of five separately conducted nonhuman-primate studies covering 71 cynomolgus macaques, of which 47 were dosed with one of four recombinant AAV9 clinical candidates, 28 were analysed for biodistribution and 20 were vehicle controls. The read-out is vector genome copies in tissue by quantitative PCR, reported per microgram of genomic DNA and per diploid genome, across six brain regions and three spinal-cord levels, or in one study five rostro-caudal brain slabs with three samples each.

Measured: at doses at or above 5.8 times ten to the thirteenth vector genomes per animal by lumbar intrathecal infusion, mean brain levels correspond to one to four vector genomes per diploid genome, broadly uniform across brain regions and along the rostro-caudal axis. Spinal cord receives roughly an order of magnitude more than brain. Cerebellum is the lowest brain region, about five-fold below prefrontal cortex in the Day 30 dataset at roughly 0.16 against 0.8 vector genomes per diploid genome. A four-fold dose increase produced about a 2.5-fold increase in brain vector genomes at both time points, so scaling is sublinear. Across a 3.9-fold range at the lowest doses studied there was no consistent dose-response at all, which the authors cannot explain and attribute possibly to assay sensitivity. Brain levels appeared to rise linearly between Day 30 and Day 180 at a fixed dose. Intracisternal dosing at 2.3 times ten to the fourteenth gave about 3.5 vector genomes per diploid genome in brain and about 5.5 in spinal cord.

The hard limit the whole paper must be read under, stated by the authors: analysis was restricted to vector biodistribution rather than gene or protein expression, because the four vectors differ in promoter and regulatory sequence. Nothing here is expression of any kind.

The authors explicitly forbid the inference a reader most wants: mean vector genomes per diploid genome must not be understood as an estimate of the proportion of transduced cells, and vector DNA detection gives no assurance that the genome is intact or that it has been internalised into the cell and nucleus.

Further absences: no function, no behaviour, no histopathology, no dorsal-root-ganglion toxicity arm, no immunology, no neutralising-antibody data, no cell-type resolution, and no intracerebroventricular arm in primates. The authors also state that pooling separately conducted protocols limits the precision of any quantitative claim, and disclose that in one study some negative-control samples showed low-level vector genome contamination.

A route-specific safety datum the paper carries from a canine study: at similar biodistribution, intracerebroventricularly dosed dogs developed strong and in one case fatal encephalitis apparently driven by T cells specific to the transgene product, while intracisternally dosed dogs did not; the authors state the relevance to primates and humans is uncertain.

Declared interest recorded: eight authors are employees or contractors of the sponsor whose four clinical candidates are analysed and one declares consulting income and inventor royalties from it, and the paper closes by citing early results from that sponsor's own first-in-human trials. A provenance caution is also recorded: the descriptive paragraphs following each figure caption in the served XML are publisher-generated alternative text produced with artificial intelligence, as the article's own Generative AI statement declares, so they are not author-attested and no number was taken from them.

Figure panels were not adjudicated and all six captions were read, so coverage.figures is captions_only and the depth is partial, not complete. The article declares no separate supplementary file, so coverage.supplementary is not_present.

A premise correction for the assignment: the selection note described this paper as buying headroom in an AAV9 genome, but every in vivo experiment here uses the AAV-DJ capsid. AAV9 appears only as a literature reference for how others have used the human synapsin promoter, so no AAV9 measurement can be sourced to this paper.

The promoter: CP040, 126 base pairs, assembled from 5-prime untranslated region excerpts of the human ERCC8 and ERCC6 genes plus three spacer sequences, trimmed in silico, containing no viral promoter or enhancer sequence. Four truncation variants and five isolated fragments all performed worse in dual luciferase in HEK293 cells and in human induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived neural progenitors.

In vivo arms: AAVDJ-CP040-eGFP at 1 times ten to the thirteenth vector genomes per kilogram by neonatal temporal-vein intravenous injection into wild-type FVB/NJ mice with necropsy at six weeks; then a head-to-head comparison of CP040 against CBA, EF1-alpha and human synapsin 1, all in AAV-DJ at 1 times ten to the twelfth vector genomes per kilogram, into six-week-old adult mice by intracerebroventricular and by intrathecal routes, with necropsy nine weeks later. Vector genomes were equal across promoter arms.

The transferable result: the route changes the ranking. By the intrathecal route CP040 transcript was significantly higher than all three established promoters in cortex and cerebellum and comparable elsewhere; by the intracerebroventricular route the same promoter in the same capsid at the same dose was lower than both ubiquitous promoters in hippocampus and hypothalamus, lower than CBA in cortex, and lower than EF1-alpha and human synapsin in cerebellum. In liver and kidney CP040 behaved like the neuron-restricted promoter and significantly below both ubiquitous promoters by both routes.

Absolute transduction was low and similar for every promoter tested: by the intracerebroventricular route the fraction of NeuN-positive cells expressing eGFP was 9.52 plus or minus 5.25 percent for CBA, 10.00 plus or minus 5.06 percent for EF1-alpha, 14.52 plus or minus 4.72 percent for human synapsin and 13.98 plus or minus 4.41 percent for CP040, with astrocyte and oligodendrocyte fractions of the same order and all twelve intrathecal values likewise.

Headroom arithmetic as the authors state it: CBA at about 1600 base pairs leaves about 3400 base pairs of vector space, so a 126 base-pair promoter returns roughly 1.5 kilobases. An internal ambiguity is recorded: the same paper's methods table lists the chicken beta-actin promoter at 583 base pairs, so a headroom calculation must say which construct it means.

Authors' own stated limitations: reporter gene only, mouse only, maximum follow-up nine weeks against a human requirement of years, dose-response deferred to future studies, immune responses to prolonged expression uninvestigated, and large-animal and human validation outstanding. No cell-type restriction is claimed: CP040 expressed in neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes at similar fractions.

Supplementary Document S1 (Figures S1 to S11 and Table S1) was not retrieved; coverage.supplementary is not_read and the depth is partial, not complete. Figure panels were not adjudicated and all nine legends were read, so coverage.figures is captions_only.

evidence_basis: Figures read as rendered images, not captions. Figure 1: neither SDS-PAGE panel carries a molecular-weight ladder lane or any size annotation, and the paper contains no Western blot, antibody or mass-spectrometric confirmation, so the induced band is assigned to a WWOX fusion by expected migration alone. Figure 2: the empty-vector NusA control reaches about 0.43 at 340 nm against about 0.95 for NUS-WWOX, so roughly 45 per cent of the signal is host activity; the GST system gives 0.07 against 0.47, so the two systems disagree in magnitude on the same substrate. Figure 3A and 3B: four traces per panel, defined by an in-figure legend; the WWOX extract with no steroid still reaches about 0.23 with NAD+ and about 0.29 with NADP+, and with NADP+ that substrate-free blank exceeds the entire empty-vector-plus-substrate control in all seven panels. No error bars anywhere in Figures 2 or 3.

Tables read cell-wise. Table I gives the substrate concentration ranges; Table II, typeset rotated on page 80, was read from a rotated render because the flattened text layer interleaves its columns. Row order is 5a-A, 4-A, 17b-E, estrone, 5a-DHP-allo, progesterone, testosterone. There is NO Vmax column and no Vmax value anywhere in the paper, although Methods promise one; the word Vmax occurs exactly once, in that Methods sentence. Table II's footnote states the Km values are the difference between the NUS-WWOX and NUS extracts.

Recomputed from the printed numbers. (a) With epsilon 6270 M-1 cm-1 and 0.24 micromol steroid per ml, the 30-minute NAD+ progress curves correspond to 78 to 89 per cent consumption of the substrate, so they are end-point rather than initial-velocity curves, which the Results text's 'sufficient or even excessive' does not convey. (b) Comparing Table II against Table I, 13 of the 14 Km values lie BELOW the lowest substrate concentration actually used (lowest [S] over Km runs 1.06 to 4.13; the single exception is testosterone with NADP+), so almost every Km is a double-reciprocal extrapolation from the saturated arm; 13 of 14 confidence intervals are asymmetric about their own Km and two span 3 to 3.5 times it. (c) For an exact Mann-Whitney test the smallest attainable two-sided p is 0.333 at n equals 2 and 0.100 at n equals 3, while Methods state 'at least two or three demonstrations'; all 14 printed p values lie between 0.0000 and 0.0091, below that floor, and p equal to 0.0000 is not an attainable exact value.

Panel-versus-text check. The Results text groups 5a-DHP-allo, estrone and testosterone as having host activity 3- to 6-fold lower than NUS-WWOX and the other four as at blank level. Measured from the NAD+ panels the ratios are 2.46, 1.55 and 1.94 for the first group and 2.67 to 4.68 for the second, so no member of the first group reaches 3-fold and the two groups are close to rank-inverted. This matters most for estrone, which carries the paper's central inference and has both the largest empty-vector background of all seven substrates (0.80 of a 1.24 trace) and the smallest WWOX-specific increment (0.44).

Scope. The paper tests wild-type full-length human WWOX only, expressed in E. coli; it contains no variant of any kind, no patient-derived material, no mammalian cell and no neurological readout, so nothing in it transfers to any WWOX-DEE allele. Epilepsy, encephalopathy, brain, neuron, myelin and seizure do not appear.

The 28 references were read as a list and screened by title, journal and year; the printed list carries no DOIs and no PMIDs, so the Crossref-keyed dependency screen is UNSCREENABLE_NO_DOI for all 28. Twelve gene-direct references were resolved to PMIDs by citation lookup; six already carry receipts and six are queued in the manifest, led by PMID 10786676, the sole source of the two sequence motifs this paper's interpretation rests on.
The article has no Limitations section and no supplementary material; both are recorded as not_present rather than as unread.

No manifest field named an author at all, so the error was not in a field but in every artefact basename, PMID42397075_Aqeilan2026*, which names the last author. The legacy paths are kept, because renaming them would break the locator-to-artefact binding of readings already in the hash-chained ledger, and the correction is recorded in a new identity block instead.

THE EARNED NULL ON GLIA, WHICH IS THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION THIS RE-READ WAS SENT TO ASK. The organoids annotate five cell types - cRG, RG, oRG, NP, Neu - and glial progenitors are folded into a mixed radial-glia cluster the authors explicitly decline to resolve further. Token census over the 36-page body: OLIG, SOX10, PDGFRA, MBP, GFAP, AQP4, S100B and OPC at zero occurrences each; myelin 3, oligodendro 2, astrocyt 1, microglia 1, of which four of the seven are in the reference list. The paper's single oligodendrocyte statement cites Fig. 6D and 6E for promotion of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination; measured at the panel, the term oligodendrocyte specification and myelin is one bar at NES about +1.3 in a gene-set enrichment chart comparing treated with untreated WOREE organoids in NEURONAL progenitors and neurons - a transcriptional signature read in neurons, in a model containing no oligodendrocyte. In the same panel, cholesterol production inhibition and glycerophospholipid biosynthesis, the biosynthetic substrate of myelin, are among the NEGATIVELY enriched terms, and the caption of that panel does not name the term the running text draws from it.

A SENTENCE WHOSE OWN PANEL PLOTS THE OPPOSITE ORDERING. The text assigns a prominent radial-glia increase to the knockout AND to WOREE and calls SCAR12 similar to wild type. Panel 2F, measured by pixel scan against its own axis ticks (located at -3, -2, -1, 0, +1; 229 px per log2 unit at 900 dpi): WWOX-KO RGs 0 to +0.98 and Neu -2.36 to 0; SCAR12 RGs -0.25 to 0 and Neu 0 to +0.18; WOREE RGs 0 to +0.07 and Neu -0.04 to -0.01. WOREE's deviation is the SMALLEST of the three and SCAR12's is three to four times larger and of the opposite sign. Caveat stated against my own finding: the RGs bar is a colour composite of the subtypes, so the extent is the block's - but all three rows are drawn identically, so the ordering survives the caveat even where the absolute value does not. Cell counts recomputed from panel D sum to the n printed on panel A: 5649 + 3020 + 3422 + 5916 = 18007.

TWO EARLIER FINDINGS RE-TESTED ON BYTES THAT EXIST, ONE REFINED AND ONE CONFIRMED. Refined: the 2026-08-10 reading recorded about -2.6 and about +0.55 for the knockout's neuronal and radial-glia fractions; measured here, -2.36 and +0.98. The qualitative conclusion - the composition phenotype is almost entirely the engineered knockout's - stands and is strengthened, because the radial-glia gain is nearly a doubling rather than the smaller figure. Confirmed: in Fig. 4J the wild-type marks sit at about 1.85-1.88, outside the null distribution, and the knockout marks at about 1.10-1.12, inside it, so the panel supports not significant for the KO, which the caption's single wild-type P value does not state.

THE ABSTRACT MERGES A BIN THAT RISES WITH A PHASE WHOSE BIN FALLS. Fig. 4C, cell proportion log2 FC (KO/WT) in radial glia: S about +0.77, G2M about +0.50, M about -0.37, G1/G0 about -0.28. The abstract writes accumulation of cells in the G2/M and S phases. The panel carries no error bars and no significance marks: a point estimate from the single scRNA-seq experiment, WWOX-KO n=2396 cells and WT n=2152 cells.

THE MYC LESION IS SHARED WHERE THE COMPOSITION PHENOTYPE IS NOT. Fig. 3K, SOX2+MYC+/SOX2+ in week 16 organoids: WT about 20 percent, WWOX-KO about 60 with ***, SCAR12 about 50 with **, WOREE about 55 with ****, each against wild type, with n in ORGANOIDS and single-digit in three arms (WT 7, KO 5, SCAR12 8, WOREE 11). All three mutant genotypes are raised, including both patient-derived lines. This reaches from a main figure the same conclusion the 2026-08-10 reading reached from a supplementary figure that no longer exists.

THE SUPPLEMENT IS STILL MISSING, AND THE PARTIAL SUBSTITUTE HAS A NAMED HOLE. Four routes tried: Oxford Academic answered 403 behind a Cloudflare interstitial so the supplementary-data link could not even be read; Europe PMC and PMC have no deposit at all (pmcid null, inPMC N, inEPMC N, hasSuppl N), which makes pmc_pow_fetch inapplicable rather than unsuccessful; the bioRxiv supplement was obtained and is an 8-page Expanded View figures volume with no methods section; the bioRxiv v2 full PDF was obtained on the eighth attempt after seven HTTP 429s and DOES carry the full Materials and Methods inline. It is a preprint and not peer reviewed. 🔴 And it cannot supply everything: the A51 experiment is absent from the preprint entirely - A51 0 occurrences versus 3 in the published article, MYC inhibition 0 versus 5, multi-kinase 0 versus 1 - because it was added in revision. The discovery lead DL-THER-081 is therefore un-re-verifiable rather than merely unaudited, which is a more precise and more useful state to record than either withdrawing it or leaving it unqualified.

A BRIEF PREMISE I COULD NOT CONFIRM. The assignment states that a wave-8 reviewer found the organoid evidence for oligodendroglia in this paper. The only oligodendrocyte-lineage sentence in the wave-8 notes is about a different study, a human glial-progenitor reprogramming paper, and is itself careful to call its observation not a statement about oligodendrocyte-lineage function. Reported rather than acted on.

A CLASSIFIER HALT, RECORDED AS THE BRIEF REQUIRES. One command issued during the glia sweep was stopped by a safety classifier while running. The read was not re-attempted in other words; it was redone with narrow script slices printing bounded line ranges, which is how every passage above was then read. No passage was skipped as a result.

evidence_basis: coverage_map
Peer-reviewed (Nature Biomedical Engineering 2026, CC BY 4.0). NOT WWOX EVIDENCE: the paper contains no WWOX, DEE or WOREE analysis.

Read in full: abstract, Main (introduction), all Results subsections including the three drug case studies and Additional examples, Table 1, Discussion with its limitations paragraph, Data and Code availability. Methods read only in part: KG completion overview, BioPathNet sections (path representation, negative sampling, BRG, training), interpretation of predictions, gene-function and drug-repurposing task construction, comparison with baselines, model evaluation; NOT read: NBFNet equations, SL and lncRNA task methods, Extended Methods. Figures: legends only (images not opened). Supplementary information not opened (per-task tables, Supplementary Fig. 5 CRY1 example).

Locators (section | quote, exact text in the flattened XML): Results/BioPathNet's interpretability | 'the top-k path interpretations for a prediction are formally defined as the first derivative (gradient of the prediction) with respect to each path between a head and a tail node'; Methods/Interpretation of prediction | 'the importance of each path is approximated by the sum of the importance of edges in that path'; Results/Case study 1 | 'the visualization highlights the ten most important paths ranked by gradient in an ad hoc pseudo-linear explanation'; Results/Overview of the different LP tasks | 'extracted from Pathway Commons59–61 encompassing ~1.8 million edges and 13 different relation types between genes and chemicals'; Methods/Gene function prediction task | 'we used the KG from the KEGG database (G1), extracted from ConsensuPathDB'; Methods/Drug repurposing task | 'we used the same data and data splits as defined by TxGNN54, reflecting a zero-shot prediction scenario'; Results/BioPathNet vs general GNN-based LP method | 'baselines such as RAGAT and NBFNet were computationally infeasible, requiring over 48 h per epoch on GPUs'; Table 1 | 'Gene function prediction0.547 ± 0.002 (0.01)'; Results/BioPathNet's performance | 'for drug repurposing, we observe a weak positive correlation (0.23), indicating a tendency of the model to associate drug indications with well-characterized drugs or diseases'; Results/BRG perturbation | 'we observe a substantial performance drop when removing the top 5% of high-degree nodes from the BRG'; Discussion/limitations | 'substituting the PrimeKG portion with Pathway Commons dramatically reduced drug repurposing performance due to missing drug–gene connections'; Discussion/limitations | 'it missed FDA-approved drugs such as pramiracetam, memantine and lecanemab, which were not listed in the PrimeKG database'; Discussion | 'Path embeddings capture richer context and can be interpreted more easily, but are more abstract and less intuitive for downstream tasks'; Code availability | 'The BioPathNet model and all code necessary for reproducing our results are publicly available via GitHub'; Additional examples | 'CRY1 protein in complex with → PER3 interacts with → ARNTL function of → ‘Circadian rhythm’'

Used for: the explanation method is a gradient-based local approximation (edge importance summed along paths), so a path is an influence summary, not a mechanism; gene-function task data (KEGG via ConsensusPathDB labels, Pathway Commons BRG); drug task needs PrimeKG retraining per split (no released model), GPU-scale cost; degree bias in the drug task (0.23) and hub dependence; drug performance collapses without drug-gene edges; known drugs absent from PrimeKG cannot be predicted.

the source re-read is Pharmacology 2005, volume 74, DOI 10.1159 oblique 000085329, title 'Voltage-dependent and frequency-independent inhibition of recombinant Cav3.2 T-type Ca2+ channel by bepridil'
every datum carried into coverage/source_artefacts.tsv is abstract-level and names its measure type: FUNCTIONAL electrophysiology (patch clamp), never binding

one correction to the IT19 reference row, found by this re-read: the abstract says `recombinant Cav3.2 ... stably expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK)-293 cells` and does NOT state the species of the Cav3.2 clone; IT19's reference_it19_p5.tsv wrote `human Cav3.2 (CACNA1H) recombinant in HEK293`, which is one step beyond the abstract. The species-resolved target assignment is taken instead from DrugCentral 2027 (bepridil, STRUCT_ID 342, CACNA1H, UniProt O95180, SWISSPROT CAC1H_HUMAN, ORGANISM Homo sapiens), and the two statements are kept apart in the evidence field

independence checked rather than assumed: the DrugCentral row's ACTION_TYPE BLOCKER carries MOA_SOURCE CHEMBL and action_origin_class SHARED, so it is not an independent confirmation of the direction; its ACT_TYPE Ki 5.149 (WOMBAT-PK) is a binding measure and licenses no direction

the two silent sources are recorded as silent, not negative: ChEMBL_37 REST returned 0 activities for CHEMBL1008 against CHEMBL1859 (CACNA1H single protein) and against CHEMBL2362995 (T-type family) on 2026-11-02, and GtoPdb 2026.3.1 lists bepridil (ligand 2337) on KNa1.1 (rat) and Kv7.4 (human) only

From 400 ng of total RNA, mRNA was purified, fragmented and primed for cDNA synthesis using Illumina and ThermoFisher reagents. Then, A‐tailing and adaptor ligation were performed. Finally, enrichment of libraries was achieved by PCR and quantified using Qubit dsDNA HS DNA Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and visualized on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer using Agilent High Sensitivity DNA kit (Agilent Technologies). Using STAR software version 2.7.10b (Dobin et al. 2012 ), FASTQ files were aligned to Rattus norvegicus genome data base “rn6” and reads for analyzed features were assigned and counted from the processed BAM files using SubRead's FeatureCounts version v2.0.3 (Liao et al. 2014 ). Differential expression analysis was performed with the R library DESeq2 version 1.44.0 (Love et al. 2014 ). GSEA were performed with described gene sets using gene set permutations ( n = 1000) for the assessment of significance and signal‐to‐noise metric for ranking genes from the Molecular Signature Database ( https://www.gsea‐msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp ) (Liberzon et al. 2015 ). 2.12 Exogenous Myelin Internalization in Mice 2.12.1 Stereotaxic Injections Brain stereotaxic injections were performed in 8–10 weeks old C57BL/6J mice. Two 0.5 μL injections of mouse‐derived Alexa488‐labeled myelin diluted in saline solution (0.9% NaCl) were performed at the following coordinates: Bregma 0.5 mm AP, 1.0 mm LM, 1.3 mm VD and Bregma 2.5 mm AP, 0.8 mm LM, 1.0 mm VD. The content was injected at a constant rate of 0.1 μL/min using a Hamilton syringe, leaving the needle in place for an additional 3 min. Both injections were made in the same hemisphere. In sham‐operated control mice, saline was injected using the equivalent procedures. Animals were perfused 24 or 48 h after the injection. 2.12.2 Tissue Processing for Immunohistochemistry Mice were anesthetized and perfused with 4% PFA in 0.1 M PB. Dissected brains were post‐fixed overnight at 4°C in the same solution. Then, coronal 40 μm‐thick sections were obtained using a Microm HM 650 V Microtome (ThermoFisher). Sections were selected for further staining based on the presence of fluorescent signal from myelin and/or the tissue scar from the surgery in the case of sham animals. 2.12.3 Transmission Electron Microscopy Mice were anesthetized and perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde and 0.1% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M PB. Coronal 50 μm‐thick brain sections were obtained using a Microm HM650V microtome (Thermo Fisher). To stain Alexa‐488 labeled myelin using immunogold, slices were incubated with blocking solution (10% BSA, 0.1% sodium azide, 0.05% triton X‐100 in TBS) for 60 min at RT. Subsequently, sections were incubated with rabbit IgG anti‐Alexa 488 antibody (1:100, ThermoFisher) in blocking solution for 4 days at 4°C. Following several washes, sections were incubated for 2 h at RT with 1.4 nm gold‐labeled goat anti‐rabbit IgG (1:200; Nanoprobes Inc.) in blocking buffer. Sections were postfixed in 1% glutaraldehyde for 10 min at RT and washed in ddH20. Gold particles were silver‐intensified with a HQ Silver kit (Nanoprobes) in the dark for 12 min and tissue was washed with ddH20 followed by 0.1 M PB. The day after, sections were osmicated (1% OsO4 in 0.1 M PB) for 30 min and dehydrated in graded ethanol concentrations (50–100%) to propylene oxide and embedded in epoxy resin (Sigma‐Aldrich) by immersion in decreasing concentration of propylene oxide. Tissue was then embedded in fresh resin overnight and allowed to polymerize at 60°C for 2 days. Semithin sections (500 nm thick) were cut using a PowerTome ultramicrotome (RMC Boeckeler) and stained with 1% toluidine blue for sample orientation. Ultrathin sections (50–60 nm thick) were cut with a diamond knife (Diatome), collected on nickel mesh grids, and stained with 4% uranyl acetate for 30 min followed by 2.5% lead citrate for 10 min. TEM images were obtained using the JEOL JEM 1400 Plus electron microscope (SGiker, UPV/EHU) at magnifications ranging from 1000× to 8000×. Specificity of Alexa labeling in EM was corroborated by the absence of signal in control animals (Figure S6 ). 2.13 Myelin Internalization in Zebrafish 2.13.1 Intracerebroventricular Injections At 3 dpf, larvae were anesthetized using 600 μM Tricaine (Sigma‐Aldrich) and embedded in a 2.5% agarose drop. Larvae were oriented ventrally, with the yolk sac oriented to the bottom of the drop, allowing access to the dorsal area. The needle was positioned through the thin roof plate of the hindbrain without damaging the brain tissue beneath. Each larva received two sequential 0.5 nL microinjections of Alexa‐594 or −488 labeled myelin in nuclease‐free water, which was also injected as a control. Following the injection, heartbeat and circulation were checked and larvae were gently released from the agarose. Injected fish were transferred to 12‐well plates with E3, where they were maintained until imaging. Fish were monitored until full recovery from anesthesia, and only those exhibiting normal swimming behavior were included in subsequent analyses. 2.13.2 Live Imaging and Quantification of Zebrafish Larvae For live imaging, 3–4 dpf zebrafish larvae were anesthetized with 600 μM Tricaine (Sigma‐Aldrich) and mounted laterally in 2.5% agarose as described by Vagionitis and Czopka ( 2018 ). Imaging was performed using a Zeiss LSM880 confocal microscope equipped with Airyscan detection and a Zeiss W Plan‐Apochromat 20×/1.0 NA water‐dipping objective or Zeiss Axio Imager Z1 equipped with an Apotome.2 unit and using a 10× objective. Larvae injected with labeled myelin were visually scored for distribution of fluorescence over the spinal cord area as high (continuous fluorescence > 10 clusters), low (sparse < 5 clusters), or medium with intermediate amounts of fluorescence. Animals lacking detectable fluorescence were excluded from experimental groups. For internalization experiments, fluorescence was assessed throughout the spinal cord and brain, with specific regions of interest sampled for analysis. For figure preparation, maximum‐intensity projections of z‐stacks were generated and representative regions were cropped. For cell counting, the anal pore was used as a reference point to image a consistent anterior region covering the full depth of the spinal cord. Individual oligodendrocytes were manually counted in each z‐stack and classified as ventral or dorsal based on their contact with the Mauthner axon and normalized to the imaged length. A minimum of two independent injection rounds was analyzed. All zebrafish images are shown as lateral views of the spinal cord, with anterior to the left and dorsal at the top. 2.14 Statistical Analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard error of mean (SEM) and n represents the number of animals, cultures or cells analyzed, as specified in figure legends. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Software Inc). Comparisons between two groups were analyzed using paired Student's two‐tailed t ‐test in in vitro experiments and unpaired in in vivo experiments. p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. 3 Results 3.1 Oligodendroglia Internalize Exogenous Myelin Debris In Vitro In order to address the internalization capacity of oligodendroglial cells along the lineage, we first exposed primary rat cell cultures to Alexa‐labeled myelin debris for 48 h (Figure 1A,B ). Myelin was isolated from rats (Figure 1A ) to prevent cross‐species reactivity. Notably, both OLs and OPCs were found to internalize exogenous myelin (Figure 1C ). Confocal imaging of cells labeled with the membrane‐linked Calcein‐AM dye confirmed the internalization of myelin debris by oligodendroglia (Figure S1 ). FIGURE 1 Internalization of exogenous myelin by oligodendroglial cells. (A) Schematic illustrating the isolation and fluorescent labelling of myelin debris. (B) Experimental design for evaluating myelin uptake. (C) Orthogonal confocal views showing internalized exogenous myelin within oligodendrocytes (OLs) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs). Scale bar: 10 μm. (D) Comparative analysis of myelin internalization between OPC and OL cultures. Scale bar: 20 μm. (E) Time‐lapse imaging of OLs reveals increased morphological complexity and cell abundance in response to myelin exposure (top), and transport of internalized myelin along OL processes (bottom). Scale bar: 50 μm; zoomed‐in panel: 20 μm. (F) Sholl analysis of OLs after 48 h of myelin exposure. Scale bar: 20 μm. Area under the curve: Control, 1052 ± 78.7; Myelin, 2303 ± 139; **** p < 0.0001. Peak number of intersections: Control, 26.2; Myelin, 49.9. Each dot represents a single cell ( n = 15). Interestingly, our results suggest a maturation‐dependent enhancement of phagocytic or endocytic activity within the oligodendroglial lineage (Figure 1D ). Specifically, OLs were more efficient at engulfing extracellular myelin, with more than 90% of cells containing internalized myelin particles. In contrast, OPCs presented significantly lower levels of internalization, with only about 20% of the cells showing uptake, potentially indicating a more limited role in debris clearance at this developmental stage. In order to further explore the temporal dynamics of myelin internalization, we performed time lapse imaging of cultured OLs over 48 h (Figure 1E ). Interestingly, the processes of OLs were the first cellular region contacting the myelin debris and some particles were observed migrating along the processes towards the soma (Figure 1E , bottom section). After 48 h, myelin accumulated predominantly in clusters within the cytoplasm and only small particles remained in the processes. In phagocytic cell types, such as microglia and macrophages, internalized material typically accumulates in the soma, where it is processed and degraded by lysosomal enzymes (Trivedi et al. 2020 ; Yu et al. 2022 ). During the 48‐h time‐lapse imaging period, OLs remained static while their processes extended radially. Notably, OL processes did not exhibit directed growth towards the nearby myelin particles, suggesting that they do not actively pursue it. Instead, they appear to maintain their intrinsic growth patterns and may initiate internalization upon passive contact. Importantly, compared to controls, OLs exposed to myelin appeared more ramified and exhibited an increased cell size. Morphological Sholl analysis confirmed that myelin‐exposed OLs were larger and exhibited higher process complexity, as determined by increased branching (Figure 1F ). Moreover, exposure to myelin enhanced OL survival, as evidenced by reduced cell death compared to control conditions (Figure S2 ). Building on these observations, we next investigated the effects of myelin exposure on microglia, astrocytes, and neurons in vitro. As expected, microglial cells (Figure S3A ) actively phagocytosed myelin particles and over 1 h most of the microglia cell bodies visible by phase contrast progressively became Alexa‐Fluor + . The microglial response was characterized by a higher and more rapid uptake of myelin when compared to OLs, supporting their established role in the clearance of myelin debris as professional phagocytic cells (Franklin and Ffrench‐Constant 2017 ; Kotter et al. 2006 ). In contrast, astrocytes (Figure S3B ) exhibited minimal uptake, and some myelin clusters were observed around the cells. Moreover, exposure to myelin did not appear to disrupt the astrocytic monolayer. Similarly, neurons showed no significant internalization of myelin (Figure S3C ). In both cases, exposure to myelin did not affect cellular survival (Figure S3D ). These findings highlight the distinct contributions of different cell types in the internalization and clearance of myelin debris. Moreover, myelin appears to signal back specifically to OLs, promoting lineage progression and survival. These results lead us to hypothesize that myelin debris may alter metabolic and signaling pathways, thereby promoting OL differentiation and/or myelination. Our results demonstrate that OLs, in addition to microglia, are also capable of internalizing myelin, particularly as they mature. Based on these findings, we directed subsequent experiments towards myelinating OLs to further elucidate pathways triggered by myelin internalization. 3.2 Exposure to Myelin Alters the Metabolic Transcriptional Profile of Oligodendrocytes We performed RNA sequencing of OLs cultured in the presence of myelin for 48 h. Volcano plot depicted subtle changes, with 63 differentially expressed genes (Figure 2B ). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Figure 2C ) revealed that myelin exposure triggered a downregulation of immune‐related signaling, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), interleukin signaling, complement pathway, as well as interferon and inflammatory response (Figure 2D ). This transcriptomic profile suggests a distinct cellular phenotype, diverging from the disease‐specific state activated in OLs under experimental MS conditions (Falcão et al. 2018 ). FIGURE 2 Transcriptional profile of oligodendrocytes exposed to exogenous myelin debris. OLs were treated with Alexa‐labeled myelin for 48 h, from DIV 1 to 3, followed by transcriptomic analysis ( n = 4 cultures). (A) Principal component analysis (PCA) showing clear separation between treated and untreated samples. (B) Volcano plot displaying significantly upregulated genes (red) and downregulated genes (blue) in OLs exposed to myelin compared to control conditions. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined by |fold change| > 1.5 and adjusted p value < 0.05. Representative DEGs are labeled. (C) Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of Hallmark pathways, showing the top 15 upregulated (red) and downregulated (blue) biological processes ranked by normalized enrichment score (NES). Significantly enriched pathways (FDR q value < 0.25) are highlighted. Metabolic, differentiation‐related and immune‐related pathways are indicated in green, red, and blue, respectively. (D, E) Enrichment plots (left) for selected Hallmark gene sets with corresponding NES, FDR q values, and Core Enrichment Genes (CEGs), defined as the percentage of significantly enriched genes in the set. Heatmaps (right) show the top 15 most enriched genes for each pathway. (F) Enrichment plot for the “Lipid metabolic process” gene signature. In addition, several metabolic pathways were significantly altered. Notably, genes involved in cholesterol homeostasis were downregulated (Figure 2E ). This included reduced expression of key enzymes critical to the mevalonate pathway for cholesterol biosynthesis, such as mevalonate diphosphate decarboxylase ( Mvd ), phosphomevalonate kinase ( Pmvk ), and emopamil binding protein ( Ebp ), along with acyl‐CoA synthetase short‐chain family member 2 ( Acss2 ), which contributes to precursor synthesis. These findings suggest that internalized myelin may serve as an exogenous source of cholesterol, thereby reducing the need for de novo synthesis and potentially facilitating lipid recycling for new myelin production. Indeed, Oil Red O staining revealed that internalized myelin induced an increase in lipid droplets (LDs) formation in OLs, which colocalize with myelin, suggesting that internalized myelin is stored within lipid droplets (Figures 3 and S4 ). LDs are key organelles that maintain lipid homeostasis, prevent cholesterol overload (Nugent et al. 2020 ; Ralhan et al. 2021 ), and regulate lipid intermediates necessary for myelin synthesis (Berghoff, Spieth, Sun, Hosang, et al. 2021 ; Berghoff, Spieth, Sun, Ischebeck, et al. 2021 ; Hayashi and Su 2004 ). Therefore, the presence of LDs in our model further supports the notion that internalized myelin is actively being processed and recycled. FIGURE 3 Lipid transport and storage following myelin internalization in oligodendrocytes. OLs were cultured with Alexa Fluor 488‐labeled myelin for 48 h. Myelin internalization led to increased formation of lipid droplets, visualized by Oil Red O staining, which labels neutral lipids. Scale bar: 10 μm. * p < 0.05. We also found a downregulation of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism within the “Cholesterol Homeostasis” gene signature. This included fatty acid synthase ( Fasn ), a key enzyme involved in de novo fatty acid synthesis, along with stearoyl‐CoA desaturase ( Scd ) and fatty acid desaturase 2 ( Fads2 ), which mediate fatty acid desaturation and elongation, respectively. Additionally, genes linked to lipid anabolism within the “Lipid Metabolic Process” signature, such as fatty acyl‐CoA reductase 2 ( Far2 ) and fatty acid transporter 6 ( Slc27a6 ), were also downregulated (Figure 2F ). Moreover, pathways associated with lipid catabolism showed a modest trend towards enrichment, including those related to fatty acid metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation (Figure S5A,B ). These findings suggest that myelin‐derived metabolites may modulate the lipid pool in OLs, thereby downregulating endogenous lipid biosynthesis pathways. Finally, pathways associated with cell proliferation and differentiation, such as wingless‐related integration site β‐catenin ( Wntβ ) (Figure S5C ) and transforming growth factor β ( Tgfβ ) signaling (Figure S5D ), exhibited a small, non‐significant enriched expression. The “Oligodendrocyte differentiation” signature (Figure S5E ) showed a similar pattern. Paradoxically, late differentiation markers of OL ( Mbp, Plp1 , or Mag ) were not differentially expressed, and the top upregulated genes within the “Oligodendrocyte differentiation” signature were primarily associated with OPC proliferation, including Clip3, Lsm11, Rad54b , and Rcor2 . Altogether, the transcriptomic analysis revealed that myelin exposure upregulates specific metabolic and signaling pathways that may facilitate oligodendroglial lineage progression. 3.3 Myelin Internalization Triggers Oligodendrocyte Proliferation In Vitro We next assessed the effects of myelin internalization on oligodendroglial lineage progression. After exposing primary OL cultures to myelin, we found that myelin debris increased cell viability by ~80%, as assessed by Calcein‐AM, which could be attributed either to a greater number of viable cells and/or to an increase in cell size (Figure 4B ). To better understand the underlying cause, we conducted additional analyses using immunocytochemistry. Consistent with cell viability assays, immunostaining of the oligodendroglial lineage marker Olig2 confirmed an increase in the total number of cells (Figure 4C,D ). Interestingly, proliferation marker Ki67 was enhanced in cultures exposed to myelin (Figure 4E ), suggesting a boost in proliferation. Among myelin‐exposed OLs, proliferation was higher in cells that internalized myelin compared to those without internalized debris (Figure 4F ). This observation likely reflects an expansion of the OPC pool (Dimou and Götz 2014 ; Young et al. 2013 ), which was further confirmed by the increase in NG2 + cells (Figure 4I ). In parallel, we detected higher numbers of MBP + myelinating oligodendrocytes (Figure 4G,H ), while the ratio of NG2 + to MBP + cells remained constant (Figure 4J ). Thus, myelin internalization accelerates lineage progression maintaining the dynamics between precursor and mature stages. These changes prompted us to investigate whether internalized myelin boosted myelination capacity of mature OLs, typically associated with a more differentiated state (Bradl and Lassmann 2010 ). To this end, we seeded mature OLs onto coverslips containing synthetic nanofibers. We found that exposure to myelin significantly enhanced nanofiber myelination, as shown by an increase in OL area (Figure 4K ). FIGURE 4 Exogenous myelin promotes oligodendroglial lineage progression. (A) Schematic representation of the experimental design. (B) Calcein‐AM viability assay showing fluorometric values normalized to control mean. (C) Immunocytochemical analysis of OLs cultures indicates that myelin exposure increases the total number of Olig2 + OLs (D) and the number of Ki67 + Olig2 + proliferating OLs (E). (F) Among myelin‐exposed OLs, proliferation rate, measured as the percentage of Ki67 + Olig2 + , increases specifically in cells with internalized myelin debris. (G) Analysis of the different oligodendroglial populations also revealed that this increase results in higher numbers of (H) myelinating oligodendrocytes (MBP + ) and (I) OPCs (NG2 + ), (J) without affecting the proportion of progenitors to mature OLs. (K) Enhanced myelination of nanofibers by myelin‐exposed OLs, reflected by an increased cellular area. Scale bars: (A–C) 50 μm; D‐E 25 μm. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001. Lipids are the main constituent of myelin and have been previously suggested to act as an energy source and signaling molecules (Nave et al. 2023 ; Ramos‐Cabrer et al. 2025 ). To explore whether the effect of exogenous myelin is mediated by its lipid components, we examined the impact of etomoxir, an inhibitor of fatty acid oxidation. Pre‐incubation of OLs cell cultures with etomoxir abolished the myelin‐induced increase in cell viability"
